board_asks: the two tangent theorems — the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact (Theorem 10.1) and the two tangents from an external point are equal (Theorem 10.2) — plus “find the length of the tangent / radius” numericals and circumscribed-figure proofs. Almost every mark here rides on those two theorems.

big_idea.tagline: One point of contact, one right angle.
big_idea.body: A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point; a secant cuts it at two. The whole chapter hangs on two facts: at the point of contact the tangent is perpendicular to the radius (Theorem 10.1), and from a point outside the circle you can draw exactly two tangents whose lengths are equal (Theorem 10.2). Together they turn tangent questions into right-triangle and congruence problems you already know how to solve.

definitions.verbatim: a tangent to a circle is a line that intersects the circle at only one point.
definitions.plain: A line that grazes the circle at a single point of contact. Contrast a secant (2 common points) and a non-intersecting line (0). The word comes from the Latin tangere, “to touch”.

definitions.verbatim: there are two common points A and B that the line PQ and the circle have. In this case, we call the line PQ a secant of the circle.
definitions.plain: A line that cuts the circle at two points. Slide a secant until its two crossing points merge into one and it becomes a tangent — that limiting idea is the bridge to the whole chapter.

definitions.verbatim: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
definitions.plain: At the point of contact, radius ⊥ tangent — a guaranteed $90°$. This right angle is the workhorse of almost every numerical and proof in the chapter (it hands you a right triangle for Pythagoras).

definitions.term: Theorem 10.2 — equal tangents from an external point
definitions.verbatim: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
definitions.plain: From a point outside, the two tangent segments are equal ($PQ = PR$). This is what powers the circumscribed-quadrilateral and inscribed-circle proofs; the centre also lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents.

definitions.verbatim: The length of the segment of the tangent from the external point P and the point of contact with the circle is called the length of the tangent from the point P to the circle.
definitions.plain: The distance from the external point to where the tangent touches the circle. With radius ⊥ tangent it is the leg of a right triangle, so $\ell = \sqrt{d^2 - r^2}$ (d = distance of the point from the centre, r = radius).

definitions.verbatim: In Fig. 10.1 (i), the line PQ and the circle have no common point. In this case, PQ is called a non-intersecting line with respect to the circle.
The common point of the tangent and the circle is called the point of contact
The tangent to a circle is a special case of the secant, when the two end points of its corresponding chord coincide.

concepts.title: A line and a circle — three positions
concepts.body: Given a circle and a line, exactly three things can happen: the line misses the circle (non-intersecting, 0 common points), cuts it at two points (secant), or touches it at one point (tangent). A tangent is the limiting case of a secant whose two crossing points have merged.

concepts.title: Tangent ⊥ radius (Theorem 10.1)
concepts.body: At the point of contact, the tangent is perpendicular to the radius. Two consequences NCERT flags in the Remarks: there is one and only one tangent at a point of a circle, and the line along that radius is called the normal at the point.
concepts.tested: cited inside almost every circle proof; the $90°$ carries the mark

concepts.title: How many tangents from a point? 0, 1 or 2
concepts.body: From a point inside the circle you can draw no tangent; from a point on the circle exactly one; from a point outside exactly two. State which case you are in before you start computing.
concepts.tested: 1-mark conceptual; sets up the length-of-tangent numericals

concepts.title: Equal tangents from an external point (Theorem 10.2)
concepts.body: The two tangents from an outside point have equal length ($PQ = PR$), so they form an isosceles triangle and the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between them. Labelling equal tangent segments from each vertex is the key move in circumscribed-figure proofs.
concepts.tested: circumscribed quadrilateral/triangle proofs, e.g. $AB+CD=AD+BC$ — Sections C/D

concepts.title: Length of a tangent — the right-triangle numerical
concepts.body: Because radius ⊥ tangent, the radius, the tangent segment and the line from the point to the centre form a right triangle. Pythagoras gives the length of the tangent $\ell = \sqrt{d^2 - r^2}$, where $d$ is the distance of the point from the centre and $r$ the radius.
concepts.tested: 2–3 mark “find the tangent length / find the radius” (Exercise 10.2 Q1, Q6)

examples.shape: Length of a tangent · NCERT Exercise 10.1 Q3
examples.problem_verbatim: A tangent PQ at a point P of a circle of radius 5 cm meets a line through the centre O at a point Q so that OQ = 12 cm. Length PQ is :

solution_steps.text: The radius $OP$ is perpendicular to the tangent $PQ$ at $P$ (Theorem 10.1), so $\triangle OPQ$ is right-angled at $P$ with hypotenuse $OQ$.

examples.mark_logic: 1-mark MCQ (Section A): radius ⊥ tangent makes $\triangle OPQ$ right-angled at $P$, then $PQ = \sqrt{OQ^2 - OP^2} = \sqrt{119}$ cm, option (D). The trap is choosing (B) 13 by adding the squares instead of subtracting.

examples.shape: Proof · NCERT Example 1 (concentric circles, chord bisected)
examples.problem_verbatim: Prove that in two concentric circles, the chord of the larger circle, which touches the smaller circle, is bisected at the point of contact.

solution_steps.text: Two concentric circles $C_1$ (larger) and $C_2$ (smaller) with centre $O$; a chord $AB$ of $C_1$ touches $C_2$ at $P$. To prove: $AP = BP$.
$AB$ is a tangent to $C_2$ at $P$ and $OP$ is its radius, so by Theorem 10.1, $OP \perp AB$.

solution_steps.lead: Perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord.
solution_steps.text: $AB$ is a chord of $C_1$ and $OP \perp AB$ passes through the centre $O$; the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so $AP = BP$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark proof (Section C): 1 for the correct set-up/figure, 1 for $OP \perp AB$ via Theorem 10.1, 1 for concluding $AP = BP$ by the perpendicular-from-the-centre-bisects-the-chord property. Not citing Theorem 10.1 by name is the common lost mark.

source.note: problem on p.149, solution runs to p.150

examples.problem_verbatim: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2∠OPQ.

solution_steps.text: Let $\angle PTQ = \theta$. By Theorem 10.2, $TP = TQ$, so $\triangle TPQ$ is isosceles.

solution_steps.lead: Base angles of the isosceles triangle.

solution_steps.text: By Theorem 10.1, $\angle OPT = 90°$, so $\angle OPQ = \angle OPT - \angle TPQ = 90° - (90° - \tfrac{1}{2}\theta) = \tfrac{1}{2}\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}\angle PTQ$. Hence $\angle PTQ = 2\angle OPQ$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark proof (Section C): 1 for $TP = TQ ⇒$ isosceles $\triangle TPQ$ (Theorem 10.2), 1 for the base angles $90° - \tfrac{1}{2}\theta$, 1 for using $\angle OPT = 90°$ (Theorem 10.1) to reach $\angle OPQ = \tfrac{1}{2}\angle PTQ$. Skipping the isosceles step breaks the angle-chase and loses marks.

examples.shape: Numerical · NCERT Example 3 (find the tangent length TP)
examples.problem_verbatim: PQ is a chord of length 8 cm of a circle of radius 5 cm. The tangents at P and Q intersect at a point T (see Fig. 10.10). Find the length TP.

solution_steps.lead: Equal tangents force a perpendicular bisector.
solution_steps.text: Join $OT$; let it meet $PQ$ at $R$. Since $TP = TQ$ (equal tangents) and $TO$ bisects $\angle PTQ$, we get $OT \perp PQ$ and $OT$ bisects $PQ$, so $PR = RQ = 4$ cm.
Right $\triangle TRP \sim$ right $\triangle PRO$ (AA), so $\dfrac{TP}{PO} = \dfrac{RP}{RO}$, i.e. $\dfrac{TP}{5} = \dfrac{4}{3}$, giving $TP = \dfrac{20}{3}$ cm.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for $PR = RQ = 4$ cm (equal tangents ⇒ $OT \perp PQ$ and bisects it), 1 for $OR = 3$ cm by Pythagoras, 1 for $TP = \tfrac{20}{3}$ cm via the similar right triangles. NCERT notes a Pythagoras route to the same $TP$.

strategies.text: Mark the point of contact and draw the radius to it — it is ⊥ to the tangent (Theorem 10.1). That $90°$ unlocks Pythagoras or a right triangle.

strategies.cue: Two tangents from one outside point?
strategies.text: They are equal (Theorem 10.2). Equal tangents ⇒ an isosceles triangle, and the centre sits on the bisector of the angle between them.

strategies.cue: Find a tangent length, radius or distance?
strategies.text: Build the radius–tangent–(line-to-centre) right triangle, then apply Pythagoras: $(\text{tangent})^2 = (\text{distance to centre})^2 - (\text{radius})^2$.

strategies.cue: Circle inscribed in a quadrilateral or triangle?
strategies.text: Label the equal tangent segments from each vertex; the opposite-side sums come out equal, e.g. $AB + CD = AD + BC$.
Inside → 0, on the circle → 1, outside → 2. State the case before you compute.

pitfalls.text: Dropping the perpendicular to the wrong point — the tangent is ⊥ to the radius only at the point of contact, not at any other point of the circle.
Adding instead of subtracting in the tangent right triangle: $(\text{tangent})^2 = OQ^2 - OP^2$, so $PQ = \sqrt{d^2 - r^2}$, never $\sqrt{d^2 + r^2}$.
Skipping the theorem citation in a proof — stating “the tangents are equal” without invoking Theorem 10.2 (or “radius ⊥ tangent” without Theorem 10.1) forfeits the reasoning mark.
Forgetting the isosceles step in an angle problem — equal tangents make the triangle isosceles; without that, the base-angle relation and the whole angle-chase collapse.

third_tab_content.name: Theorem 10.2 — the lengths of tangents from an external point are equal
third_tab_content.intro: The chapter’s workhorse result, proved by RHS congruence of the two right triangles the radii create. NCERT’s Remarks add two facts: the same result follows from the Pythagoras Theorem ($PQ^2 = OP^2 - OQ^2 = OP^2 - OR^2 = PR^2$), and since $\angle OPQ = \angle OPR$, the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents.

steps.claim: Set up what is given and what to prove.
steps.justification: A circle with centre O, a point P outside it, and two tangents PQ, PR from P. Required: PQ = PR.
OQ and OR are radii to the points of contact Q and R.

steps.claim: The radius–tangent angles are right angles.
steps.justification: Each is the angle between a radius and the tangent at its point of contact, so by Theorem 10.1 they are right angles.

steps.claim: Compare right triangles OQP and ORP.
steps.justification: OQ = OR (radii of the same circle) and OP = OP (common hypotenuse).
Right angle, hypotenuse and one side equal — RHS congruence.

steps.claim: Hence the tangent lengths are equal.
steps.justification: PQ and PR are corresponding parts of the congruent triangles (CPCT).
